claim: White matter organization has striking commonalities between different primate species.
source: In higher primates, white matter organization has striking commonalities between the different species (Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2012

claim: Several association pathways have been identified in humans, chimpanzees, and macaques.
source: Several association pathways have been identified in humans, chimpanzees, and macaques (Rilling et al., 2008; Hecht et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rilling et al., 2008 and Hecht et al., 2013

claim: White matter pathways share core properties such as the broad brain areas that they connect, but differ in the details of their branching patterns.
source: These pathways share core properties such as the broad brain areas that they connect, but differ in the details of their branching patterns, suggesting a common connectivity backbone with varying degrees of connectivity specialization.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of pathways across species

claim: Cortical regions can be described by their unique sets of connections to the rest of the brain.
source: We exploit the idea that cortical regions can be described by their unique sets of connections to the rest of the brain (Passingham et al., 2002), a feature that we have previously shown is useful in comparing brain organization between species (Mars et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Passingham et al., 2002 and Mars et al., 2016

claim: The bodies of major fiber bundles can be identified reliably in different species.
source: The bodies of the major fiber bundles can be identified reliably in different species and allow identification of homologous fiber bundles.
evidence: Based on the authors' knowledge and methodology

claim: 39 tracts common across both species were defined and reconstructed using probabilistic tractography.
source: (a) 39 tracts common across both species were defined and reconstructed using probabilistic tractography.
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 1

claim: The MT+ complex is located in the ventrolateral part of the posterior temporal cortex in the human brain.
source: The MT +complex is located in the ventrolateral part of the posterior temporal cortex in the human brain (hMT+; Malikovic et al., 2016), but is located more dorsally in the ventral bank of the posterior superior temporal sulcus in the macaque monkey (Paxinos et al., 2000) (Figure 2, left panel).
evidence: Supported by citation to Malikovic et al., 2016

claim: The MT+ complex is located more dorsally in the ventral bank of the posterior superior temporal sulcus in the macaque monkey.
source: The MT +complex is located in the ventrolateral part of the posterior temporal cortex in the human brain (hMT+; Malikovic et al., 2016), but is located more dorsally in the ventral bank of the posterior superior temporal sulcus in the macaque monkey (Paxinos et al., 2000) (Figure 2, left panel).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paxinos et al., 2000

claim: hMT+ can be identified as a region of high myelin in the posterior temporal cortex that can be visualized using the ratio of T1- and T2-weighted MRI scans.
source: hMT + can be identified as a region of high myelin in the posterior temporal cortex that can be visualized using the ratio of T1- and T2-weighted MRI scans (Glasser and Van Essen, 2011; Large et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glasser and Van Essen, 2011 and Large et al., 2016

claim: The peak of hMT+ is reached by tracts associated with the visual system such as the occipital radiations and the ventral occipital fascicle, but also by longitudinal tracts such as the inferior longitudinal fascicle.
source: The peak of hMT + is reached by tracts associated with the visual system such as the occipital radiations and the ventral occipital fascicle, but also by longitudinal tracts such as the inferior longitudinal fascicle (Yeterian and Pandya, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yeterian and Pandya, 2010

claim: Comparison of connectivity blueprints identified the ventral bank of the macaque STS as most similar to human MT+.
source: We created a map of the macaque cortex indicating how different each vertex's connectivity profile was to that of a vertex in hMT+. This map showed the lowest divergence, that is highest similarity, in the ventral bank of the macaque STS, as predicted from the macaque cytoarchitectonic atlas.
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: Comparison of connectivity blueprints can identify homologous areas across brains, even when their relative location has changed.
source: Thus, comparison of connectivity blueprints can identify homologous areas across brains, even when their relative location has changed.
evidence: Inferred from the MT+ example

claim: Human pre-SMA and macaque area F6 share similar functions across the two species.
source: It has been well-established that these two regions share similar functions across the two species (Nachev et al., 2008) and can be matched based on their connectivity profiles (Sallet et al., 2013; Mars et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nachev et al., 2008, Sallet et al., 2013, and Mars et al., 2016

claim: Macaque area F6 receives widespread connections, including from the superior longitudinal fascicle, the cingulum bundle, and the frontal aslant.
source: Its connectivity fingerprint shows that it receives widespread connections, including from the superior longitudinal fascicle, the cingulum bundle, and the frontal aslant (cf. Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on data analysis and supported by citation to Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2012

claim: The KL divergence between the connectivity fingerprint of macaque F6 and each vertex of the human cortex identified an area of the human medial prefrontal cortex, anterior to the supplementary motor area proper, as most similar to macaque area F6.
source: We determined the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the connectivity fingerprint of F6 and that of each vertex of the human cortex. This map identified an area of the human medial prefrontal cortex, anterior to the supplementary motor area proper (Figure 2, right panel) and consistent with previous localizations of this area in the human (Nachev et al., 2008; Mars et al., 2016), as most similar to macaque area F6.
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: T1/T2-weighted maps partly reflect the presence of cortical myelin.
source: One such map that is easily obtainable from neuroimaging is a T1/T2-weighted map, which has been suggested to partly reflect the presence of cortical myelin (Glasser et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Glasser et al., 2014

claim: T1/T2-weighted maps show high values in primary sensory areas, low values in prefrontal and parietal association cortex, and intermediate values in frontal oculomotor areas.
source: T1/T2-weighted maps show a number of distinctive features across the human cortical hemisphere that are qualitatively similar to myelination maps, such as high values in primary sensory areas, low values in prefrontal and parietal association cortex, and intermediate values in frontal oculomotor areas.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of T1/T2-weighted maps

claim: The predicted macaque T1/T2-weighted map based on human data showed striking similarities to the actual macaque myelin map.
source: The predicted map showed striking similarities to the actual macaque myelin map (Glasser et al., 2014), replicating the high myelin in the primary visual, auditory, and sensorimotor cortex and the low myelin in the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 3

claim: The predicted macaque T1/T2-weighted map showed an intermediate level of myelin in the macaque inferior parietal cortex, whereas in reality this is an area with low myelin content.
source: For instance, the predicted map showed an intermediate level of myelin in the macaque inferior parietal cortex, whereas in reality this is an area with low myelin content.
evidence: Based on comparison of predicted and actual maps

claim: Poorer predictions are mostly located in the association cortex.
source: While this could be due to limitations in the methods, it is noticeable that the poorer predictions are mostly located in the association cortex.
evidence: Inferred from the analysis of prediction errors

claim: A large region of human inferior parietal and posterior temporal cortex, precuneus, and parts of the frontal cortex could not be predicted from any part of the macaque brain.
source: The resulting connectional dissimilarity map showed a large region of human inferior parietal and posterior temporal cortex, precuneus, and to a lesser extent parts of the frontal cortex that could not be predicted from any part of the macaque brain (Figure 4, top panel).
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The connectional dissimilarity map did not correlate with any particular aspect of the connectivity fingerprint, such as a map of the entropy of tract distribution.
source: Importantly, the between-species predictability did not correlate with any particular aspect of the connectivity fingerprint, such as a map of the entropy of tract distribution (i.e., whether a region is reached strongly by few tracts or equally strongly by multiple tracts) (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The connectional dissimilarity map overlapped with, but was different to a map of cortical expansion.
source: Similarly, the connectional dissimilarity map overlapped with, but was different to a map of cortical expansion (Van Essen and Dierker, 2007), indicating that reorganization and expansion reflect separate aspects of brain reorganization (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 4 and citation to Van Essen and Dierker, 2007

claim: Reorganization and expansion reflect separate aspects of brain reorganization.
source: Similarly, the connectional dissimilarity map overlapped with, but was different to a map of cortical expansion (Van Essen and Dierker, 2007), indicating that reorganization and expansion reflect separate aspects of brain reorganization (Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of connectional dissimilarity and expansion maps

claim: The vertex with the highest minimum KL divergence in the human brain is reached very prominently by the arcuate fascicle.
source: We compared the fingerprint of the vertex with the highest minimum KL divergence in the human brain, that is, the vertex that has the least similar match in the macaque, to the fingerprint of the most similar macaque vertices (Figure 5). This showed that this vertex is reached very prominently by the arcuate fascicle (AF).
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The vertex with the highest minimum KL divergence is located in the posterior part of the temporal cortex, an area that often shows activation in phonological or semantic tasks.
source: The vertex is located in the posterior part of the temporal cortex, an area that often shows activation in phonological or semantic tasks (Price, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Price, 2000

claim: The anterior part of the human angular gyrus receives stronger AF connectivity than its proposed macaque homolog area PG.
source: The angular gyrus has also been suggested to receive stronger AF connectivity than its proposed macaque homolog area PG (Rilling et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rilling et al., 2008

claim: Part of angular gyrus shows activation during phoneme detection.
source: This part of angular gyrus shows activation during phoneme detection (Simon et al., 2002) and has stronger grey matter density in bilinguals and adults who have learned to read compared to illiterates (Carreiras et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simon et al., 2002

claim: Part of angular gyrus has stronger grey matter density in bilinguals and adults who have learned to read compared to illiterates.
source: This part of angular gyrus shows activation during phoneme detection (Simon et al., 2002) and has stronger grey matter density in bilinguals and adults who have learned to read compared to illiterates (Carreiras et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carreiras et al., 2009

claim: Neurons in macaque area PG show visual responses.
source: Consistent with this role, neurons in macaque area PG show visual responses (Rozzi et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rozzi et al., 2008

claim: Human angular gyrus receives input from the visual word form area.
source: Human angular gyrus receives input from the visual word form area (Saygin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saygin et al., 2016

claim: The human brain contains areas with an organization not seen in the macaque in areas recruited into the language system.
source: Together, these results are consistent with the suggestion that the human brain contains areas with an organization not seen in the macaque in areas recruited into the language system.
evidence: Inferred from the analysis of connectivity differences in language-related areas

claim: The medial parietal cortex is reached by the first branch of the superior longitudinal fascicle and this innervation seems stronger in the human brain.
source: The medial parietal cortex is reached by the first branch of the superior longitudinal fascicle and this innervation seems stronger in the human brain.
evidence: Based on data analysis

claim: Medial parietal cortex area 7m is preferentially expanded in the human brain.
source: Based on shape analysis of structural imaging data of the human and chimpanzee, Bruner and colleagues have suggested that this area is preferentially expanded in the human brain (Bruner et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bruner et al., 2017

claim: The expansion of medial parietal cortex is accompanied by a change in connectivity.
source: The current results suggest that this expansion is accompanied by a change in connectivity.
evidence: Inferred from the connectivity analysis

claim: The forceps minor of the corpus callosum seems stronger in the human than in the macaque.
source: In the frontal cortex, the forceps minor of the corpus callosum seems stronger in the human than in the macaque, suggesting increased interhemispheric connectivity within the prefrontal cortex in this species.
evidence: Based on data analysis

claim: Humans have increased interhemispheric connectivity within the prefrontal cortex compared to macaques.
source: In the frontal cortex, the forceps minor of the corpus callosum seems stronger in the human than in the macaque, suggesting increased interhemispheric connectivity within the prefrontal cortex in this species.
evidence: Inferred from the stronger forceps minor in humans

claim: Regions within similar cortical systems group together in the 2D representation across species.
source: At the gross level, this showed that regions within similar cortical systems group together in the 2D representation across the species.
evidence: Based on data analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: Macaque primary visual areas 17 and 18 showed the smallest distance to human visual areas 17 and 18.
source: For instance, macaque primary visual areas 17 and 18 showed the smallest distance to human visual areas 17 and 18 and greatest to areas 24 and 25 belonging to the cingulate cortex and early sensorimotor areas 3 and 4 that do not receive any direct visual projections.
evidence: Based on data analysis

claim: Areas 23, 24, and 25, all reached by the cingulum bundle, tended to cluster together.
source: Similarly, areas 23, 24, and 25, all reached by the cingulum bundle, tended to cluster together.
evidence: Based on data analysis

claim: Monkey area 7 in the inferior parietal lobule showed smallest dissimilarity to human area 40 rather than human area 7.
source: The fact that the nomenclature of Brodmann's maps is not always consistent between species is illustrated by monkey area 7 in the inferior parietal lobule (IPL). This area showed smallest dissimilarity to human area 40 rather than human area 7.
evidence: Based on data analysis

claim: Human area 40 is located on the angular gyrus of the IPL and human area 7 belongs to the superior parietal cortex.
source: This is consistent with the location of these areas, with human area 40 located on the angular gyrus of the IPL and human area 7 belonging to the superior parietal cortex (see highlighted area in Figure 6).
evidence: Based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: The IPLs in humans and macaques are most similar to one another.
source: This result confirms earlier suggestions that the IPLs in the two species are indeed most similar to one another (cf. Mars et al. [2011]) even though human IPL receives stronger arcuate connections, as demonstrated above.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mars et al., 2011 and current data

claim: Human IPL receives stronger arcuate connections than macaque IPL.
source: This result confirms earlier suggestions that the IPLs in the two species are indeed most similar to one another (cf. Mars et al. [2011]) even though human IPL receives stronger arcuate connections, as demonstrated above.
evidence: Based on data analysis presented earlier in the manuscript

claim: Comparative atlases of different species' brains are rare in neuroscience.
source: Comparative atlases of different species' brains are rare in neuroscience, with most atlases focusing on a single species without explicit comparisons to others.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of the field

claim: Brodmann's labeling was not meant to indicate homologies.
source: Brodmann labeled cytoarchitectonic areas in both species, but the labeling was not meant to indicate homologies (Brodmann, 1909; Petrides et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brodmann, 1909 and Petrides et al., 2012

claim: An expansion map shows which areas in the human brain have disproportionally expanded compared to the macaque.
source: Earlier direct comparisons between the human and macaque cortex used surface-based registration based on a few known homologous cortical landmarks to create an expansion map showing which areas in the human brain have disproportionally expanded compared to the macaque (Van Essen and Dierker, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Van Essen and Dierker, 2007

claim: The expansion map showed areas of expansion in lateral prefrontal, inferior parietal, temporoparietal, and medial frontal cortex.
source: This map showed areas of expansion in lateral prefrontal, inferior parietal, temporoparietal, and medial frontal cortex.
evidence: Based on the expansion map from Van Essen and Dierker, 2007

claim: The connectional dissimilarity map is not an expansion map, but rather a map of connectional reorganization.
source: Our connectional dissimilarity map is not an expansion map, but rather a map of connectional reorganization.
evidence: Based on the authors' interpretation of their results

claim: The connectional dissimilarity map and expansion map describe separate aspects of cortical specialization.
source: Thus, the two maps describe separate aspects of cortical specialization, both of which are important in understanding what makes any one brain unique.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of the two types of maps

claim: Four post-mortem macaque diffusion MRI datasets were used.
source: Four post-mortem macaque diffusion MRI datasets were used.
evidence: Described in the methods section

claim: Human in-vivo data was obtained from the minimally pre-processed data provided by the Human Connectome Project.
source: Human in-vivo data was obtained from the minimally pre-processed data provided by the Human Connectome Project (www.humanconnectome.org) (Van Essen et al., 2013).
evidence: Described in the methods section with citation to Van Essen et al., 2013

claim: Ten subjects were chosen randomly from the Q900 data release.
source: Ten subjects were chosen randomly from the Q900 data release.
evidence: Described in the methods section

claim: Probabilistic diffusion tractography was used to extract the anatomical blueprints of macaques and humans.
source: Probabilistic diffusion tractography (Behrens et al., 2007) as implemented in FSL's probtrackx2 was used to extract the anatomical blueprints of macaques and humans.
evidence: Described in the methods section with citation to Behrens et al., 2007

claim: An automated tractography tool was extended to include a set of 39 major white matter bundles.
source: We extended an automated tractography tool (autoPtx, De Groot et al., 2013) to include a set of 39 major white matter bundles (18 on each hemisphere, and three cross-hemispheric pathways).
evidence: Described in the methods section with citation to De Groot et al., 2013

claim: The symmetric Kullback-Leibler divergence was used as a dissimilarity measure to compare connectivity fingerprints.
source: To compare the fingerprint of vertex i in macaque to vertex j in humans, we use the symmetric Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence (Kullback and Leibler, 1951) as a dissimilarity measure
evidence: Described in the methods section with citation to Kullback and Leibler, 1951
